claims.text: Cold rolling by approximately 30–40% creates a controlled high density of dislocations without introducing excessive defects in austenitic stainless steel.
Annealing cold-worked steel at 450–500 °C for 1–2 hours facilitates solute diffusion and segregation to deformation-induced defects.
Cold working followed by low-temperature annealing enriches chromium, and potentially molybdenum, at dislocation networks and grain boundaries.
In nitrogen-added austenitic stainless steels, nitrogen segregates elastically to dislocations and promotes chromium segregation through an attractive nitrogen–chromium interaction.
Dislocations act as fast diffusion paths for chromium during annealing.
Chromium diffuses toward deformation-induced non-equilibrium defect sites during the proposed anneal.
Localized chromium enrichment at defects promotes nucleation, growth, and stabilization of a protective passive oxide film.
Chromium is important to the corrosion resistance of austenitic steels because it facilitates passive-film formation.
Molybdenum helps maintain corrosion resistance by promoting repassivation.
Passive-film integrity and repair kinetics correlate with the degree and spatial distribution of segregated alloying elements.
Cold-worked and annealed specimens will have lower corrosion-current density than both as-received and cold-worked-only specimens.
Cold-worked and annealed specimens will have higher pitting potentials than both control groups.
Cold-worked and annealed specimens will develop a more uniform and adherent passive film than both control groups.
The extent of chromium segregation will correlate positively with electrochemical corrosion resistance.
The proposed mechanism is expected to hold optimally at approximately 30–40% thickness reduction and 450–500 °C annealing for 1–2 hours.
More severe cold work or substantially higher annealing temperatures may cause excessive residual stress, grain growth, or unwanted phases that compromise corrosion resistance.
The same proposed treatment mechanism is applicable to harsh chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing as-received, cold-worked-only, and cold-worked-plus-annealed specimens under identical aerated 3.5 wt% NaCl exposure.

Failure of the combined-treatment group to show statistically significant electrochemical improvement, or failure to detect the proposed chromium segregation relationship, would falsify the hypothesis.
